title: Energy transfer and productivity; Succession; Nitrogen and phosphorus cycles
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EC06#t1 term and clue written for the game; EC07#t1 term and clue written for the game; EC06#t4 term and clue written for the game; EC07#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EC04c#N.2, EC06#N.3, EC06#N.6, EC06#N.9, EC06#N.15.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Nitrogen fixation
items.clue: Bacteria reduce N₂ from the air to NH₃

items.label: Succession
items.clue: Change over time in the species making up a community

items.label: Mutualism
items.clue: A relationship between two species in which both benefit

items.label: Climax community
items.clue: The final, stable stage, in equilibrium with its environment

questions.stem: Food chains in most ecosystems have no more than four or five trophic levels. What is the reason for this restriction?

options.text: The number of trophic levels is set by the number of species in the community, and few communities have more than five.
The tissues of organisms higher in the chain contain less energy per gram, so a predator cannot gain enough energy from each meal.
Decomposers occupy the last trophic level of every chain and take the remaining energy, so no further consumers can be added.
So much energy is lost at each transfer that after a few levels too little remains to support a viable consumer population.

questions.explanation: Most energy at each level is lost as heat or passes to decomposers, so eventually there is not enough to sustain another level.

questions.stem: Which statement about the recycling of chemical elements in ecosystems is correct?

options.text: Only carbon is recycled; the other elements are absorbed from the soil, used by organisms and then used up, so they must be replaced.
Elements are released from dead organisms automatically as they die, so decomposers play only a minor part in recycling them.
Both the chemical elements and the energy in dead organisms are recycled by decomposers and returned to producers for reuse.
All elements required by organisms are recycled; decomposers release them from dead matter in forms that autotrophs can take up.

questions.explanation: All elements used by organisms are recycled. Decomposers break down the carbon compounds of dead matter and return the elements as simple inorganic substances.

questions.stem: A field is flooded for several weeks and the soil becomes waterlogged. Afterwards, the nitrate content of the soil is much lower. Which process best explains the loss?

options.text: Nitrification, which runs faster when water fills the air spaces in the soil
Nitrogen fixation, which converts the nitrate in the soil back into nitrogen gas
Denitrification by bacteria in the anaerobic soil, giving nitrogen gas
Ammonification, in which decomposers convert the nitrate into ammonium ions

questions.explanation: Waterlogged soil is anaerobic. Denitrifying bacteria use nitrate and release N₂, which escapes to the air.

questions.stem: What are the benefits to each partner in the relationship between a legume and the bacteria in its root nodules?

options.text: The bacteria supply the plant with nitrogen gas from the soil; the plant supplies the bacteria with oxygen.
The bacteria supply the plant with fixed nitrogen as ammonia or amino acids; the plant supplies the bacteria with sugars.
The plant gains fixed nitrogen from the bacteria; the bacteria gain nothing from the plant but are not harmed by living in the nodule.
The bacteria take sugars from the roots and give the plant nothing, so the nodules are a mild infection the plant tolerates.

questions.explanation: Rhizobium in the nodules converts N₂ into ammonia, which the plant uses to make amino acids. The plant supplies sugars from photosynthesis and a protected home: both benefit.

questions.stem: A farmer grows clover, a legume, in a field for a year, then ploughs the clover into the soil. Wheat sown next needs much less nitrogen fertiliser than wheat sown after wheat. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Clover roots absorb nitrogen gas from the air in the soil, and the wheat roots then take up this same nitrogen gas.
Bacteria in the clover's root nodules fixed nitrogen gas; decomposers later released it into the soil.
The clover made new nitrogen atoms from the sugars it produced in photosynthesis, so the soil now holds more nitrogen.
The clover's own root cells fixed nitrogen gas, so no bacteria or other microorganisms were needed to enrich the soil.
